issues.title: Allowing OS to send stateless reset proactively
issues.author: lcolitti
issues.body:
Ideally it should be possible for the OS to send the stateless packet proactively, as soon as the application is placed into the background. This is a useful signal to the server that the client is gone and that if it wants to reach the client it must do so via other means (e.g., via the OS push messaging channel).

The current Android implementation sends the app-supplied close frame exactly once, and then closes the UDP socket with ECONNABORTED so the app stack gets an error. (This obviously means that if the close frame gets lost, the OS can no longer reset the connection; perhaps we could improve this.)

Perhaps we could say something like the server is allowed to proactively send the packet exactly once, to avoid looping.

issues.title: Allow OS to verify the connection ID
issues.author: lcolitti
issues.body:
The current text says "An application that is no longer permitted to send packets therefore cannot use the Stateless Reset to convey information of its own choosing." AFAICT this is not technically true because the application can specify the connection ID.

Could we say that the OS may choose not to send the stateless reset if it has not observed the application-specified connection ID in all packets received on the specified 5-tuple? Or could this break if the connection ID on the 5-tuple changes (or if - super unlikely - the app receives a garbage packet on that socket)? In that case should we say something like "the most recent received packet on the 5-tuple"?

issues.title: Who should issue the RESET_TOKEN?
issues.author: stefanoduo-google
issues.body:
> Only an endpoint that uses a zero-length Connection ID may send a RESET_TOKEN frame; the mechanism substitutes for the tokens that a Connection ID-issuing endpoint would otherwise derive from the Connection IDs it issues. An endpoint that uses a non-zero-length Connection ID MUST NOT send a RESET_TOKEN frame.

IIUC, this means that a peer, who's not issuing Connection ID is expected to be the party issuing RESET_TOKEN frame. This makes sense to maintain symmetry with how things work for a peer who's issuing Connection IDs. Let's call this peer "client" and the other one the "server".

At the same time, the client already has to also remember the connection ID, otherwise the packet might not make it to the server (due to load balancers, etc). With that in mind, I wonder if there is value in having the server issue the RESET_TOKEN? This allows the server to maintain less/no state to later validate the stateless reset packet.

This would also simplify the interface between the QUIC stack and the OS/system. The QUIC stack would simply give both the Connection ID and the RESET_TOKEN to the system (possibly alongside the 5 tuple).

P.S. A possible downside of having the server issue RESET_TOKEN is that more of the packet will constructed by the QUIC stack rather than the system.

comments.author: stefanoduo-google
comments.body: We chatted offline and agreed that it's best for the peer that is not issuing connection IDs to be the one issuing the RESET_TOKEN. This will allow the other peer to handle it in the same way they handle stateless resets from peer issuing connection IDs. It also allows the system to be the one generating the token and not the QUIC stack.

issues.title: Clarify unpredictable bits for a delegated stateless reset token
issues.author: stefanoduo-google
issues.body:
Section 3.1 states:
> * the peer's Connection ID, in the position in which a 1-RTT packet carries the Destination Connection ID field (Section 4); and
> * 20 bytes that it generates at random, of which the leading 4 separate the token from the header and the trailing 16 are the Stateless Reset Token.

Section 4 states:
> When constructing a Stateless Reset, the endpoint or its delegate SHOULD place a Connection ID issued by the peer in the position in which a 1-RTT packet carries the Destination Connection ID field, rather than unpredictable bits.

To keep delegated stateless resets undistinguishable from regular packets, Section 4 should still require at least 1 unpredictable byte (section 3.1 asks for 4) between the destination connection ID and the stateless reset token.

Otherwise, an on-path observer, that knows the peer's Connection ID length, could recognize the Stateless Reset by the fact that exactly 16 bytes follow the Connection ID, and extract the token.

issues.title: Clarify operating system delegation for apps issuing Connection IDs
issues.author: stefanoduo-google
issues.body:
Section 3.1 currently states:
> The operating system exposes an interface through which an application registers, for one of its connections, a Connection ID that the peer has issued and currently accepts, together with what identifies that connection in the datagrams the peer sends -- the socket, and any Connection IDs the application itself has issued. From that registration it forms a datagram containing, in order:

If an application is issuing Connection IDs, that application must also be issuing a Stateless Reset Token alongside each Connection ID.

With that in mind, the plural (Connection IDs) and past tense can be misleading, the application should only have to give the operating system two Connection IDs for each registration:
* a Connection ID that the peer has issued and currently accepts
* the (optional) Connection ID that the application will issue, to the peer, once the operating system has returned the stateless reset token it generated during the registration procedure

The text should be updated to clarify that registration is 1-to-1 per issued Connection ID at issuance time (or per socket when zero-length Connection IDs are used).

comments.body:
I think RFC 9000 describes stateless reset as a response purely because that's the only possible way of generating them. How about:

```suggestion
Endpoints using this extension MAY send a single stateless reset packet
proactively, without waiting to receive a datagram from the peer.
{{Section 10.3 of RFC9000}} describes a Stateless Reset only as a response to a
received packet, because endpoints that have lost connection state learn of
the connection's existence only from such a packet. Endpoints using this
extension retain the Stateless Reset Token deliberately, and therefore know
which connections they may need to reset before any packet arrives.
{{os-offload}} describes a deployment in which this is useful.
```

Directionally good, but I think people would ask for the rationale behind recommending 30 seconds. Maybe something like below that would help people deduct the right value.

```suggestion
The operating system also responds to a datagram received on the registered
5-tuple by sending the same retained stateless reset, but does so only if the
stateless reset is smaller than the datagram that triggered it, as required by
{{Section 10.3.3 of RFC9000}}. This covers the case in which a stateless reset
sent proactively did not reach the peer.

Eventually, the operating system discards the stateless reset and the 5-tuple
registration, as the peer will nevertheless abandon the connection due to not
making progress.
```

pulls.title: Delegation becomes the core topic
pulls.author: kazuho
pulls.body:
The document started as a description of a mechanism missing from RFC 9000: issuing Stateless Reset Tokens when Connection IDs are not used. But we have since been adding text about how stateless resets can be delegated to a component that outlives the QUIC stack, and that applies regardless of Connection ID length -- an endpoint that issues Connection IDs delegates one of the tokens it has already issued, with no new protocol at all.

It therefore seems better to change the topic of the I-D: delegation becomes the subject, and the transport parameter and frame become one section serving the case that cannot otherwise issue a token.

| before | after |
| --- | --- |
| 3. The reset_token Transport Parameter | 3. Delegating a Stateless Reset |
| 4. The RESET_TOKEN Frame | 3.1. …to the Operating System |
| 5. Sending a Stateless Reset | 4. Constructing a Routable Stateless Reset |
| 5.1. Delegating …to the Operating System | 5. Sending a Stateless Reset Proactively |
| | 6. Advertising a Token with Zero-Length Connection IDs |
| | 6.1. The reset_token Transport Parameter |
| | 6.2. The RESET_TOKEN Frame |

All the changes are editorial in nature, with one exception: the operating system registration in Section 3.1 relied solely on the 5-tuple to match datagrams to a connection, which only works where the application uses zero-length Connection IDs. It now registers the socket together with any Connection IDs the application itself has issued, so the arrangement works for a Connection ID-issuing application as well.

The document title becomes "Delegating QUIC Stateless Resets". Renaming the file and the repository to match are TODOs, kept out of this PR because file renames are not tracked well in GitHub review.

reviews.author: stefanoduo-google
reviews.body:
+1 to making delegation the core topic of the draft.

I've left a few comments, I'm happy to file issues and tackle in follow-ups if you prefer working that way.

comments.body: FYI: I've filed #7 to keep track of the diagram I would like to have for this section. I'll work on it in a follow-up.

If acting proactively, I would expect an endpoint to have enough state to send a CONNECTION_CLOSE instead. Should we scope this down to delegates?
```suggestion
A delegate MAY send a single Stateless Reset proactively,
```

Perhaps we can shuffle this text around some more? Giving some more background before flowing into the mechanics might make this easier to parse. Here is a suggested diff of what I have in mind.

(I don't feel too strongly and I'm happy to tackle this in a follow-up)

```suggestion
The same property permits a different arrangement, and it is the subject of
this document: the entity that sends a Stateless Reset need not be the endpoint
that ran the connection.

The ability to send a Stateless Reset is valuable precisely when connection state
has been lost involuntarily -- for example, when an application exits or is
terminated by the operating system. After the application is gone, the peer may
continue to send packets on the connection until its idle timeout expires. To cover
these scenarios, an endpoint can delegate the termination of the connection to a
component that outlives its own connection state, and that component can reset
the peer long after the endpoint is gone ({{delegation}}).

A CONNECTION_CLOSE packet could be recorded and used for this scenario, but
such a packet is difficult to manage for a delegate. It is protected under the
connection's packet-protection keys that endpoints periodically rotate, and it
carries a packet number that must fall within a dynamic range the peer will accept;
thus, the recorded packet would need constant refreshing to remain usable.

In contrast, sending a Stateless Reset requires only the static Stateless Reset
Token and the 5-tuple on which to send it. These remain valid until the endpoint
retires the Connection ID with which the token is associated.

A delegated Stateless Reset can also be better formed than one sent by an
endpoint that has lost its state. The delegate holds its token deliberately, and
can hold alongside it a Connection ID that the peer accepts, placing that value
where a 1-RTT packet carries the Destination Connection ID. An endpoint that has
lost its state has no such value available and must use unpredictable bits
instead, at the cost that the Stateless Reset may be misrouted ({{Section 10.3
of RFC9000}}).
```

I would explicitly call out this being the property referenced in the paragraphs that follow. This should help readers. Perhaps something along these lines?
```suggestion
continued. This mechanism relies on a specific property: the reset signal is not
protected by the connection's keys, nor is it tied to packet number spaces.
Instead, it is authenticated solely by a 128-bit Stateless Reset Token, which the
receiver matches against tokens it previously retained.
```

I feel this sentence breaks the flow from the previous one. I expect the second paragraphs to follow directly after the first sentence. Perhaps we should just drop this?
```suggestion
the Destination Connection ID field, rather than unpredictable bits.
{{Section 10.3 of RFC9000}} calls for unpredictable bits in that position
because an endpoint that has lost its state cannot recover a Connection ID that
its peer accepts, and it observes that the resulting packet "could be
incorrectly routed" where the Connection ID is critical for routing toward the
peer, as it is in load-balanced deployments. An endpoint or delegate that has
retained such a Connection ID sends a Stateless Reset that reaches the peer and
is less distinguishable from a valid packet.
```

Should we keep the text that describes the operating system proactively sending of the stateless reset?
```suggestion
Once the application is no longer able to process packets for the connection,
the operating system sends the retained datagram. The resulting datagram is
the smallest that can be mistaken for a 1-RTT packet carrying the Connection
ID that was registered.

The operating system also responds to a datagram received on the registered
5-tuple by sending the same retained stateless reset, but does so only if the
stateless reset is smaller than the datagram that triggered it, as required by
{{Section 10.3.3 of RFC9000}}. This covers the case in which a stateless reset
sent proactively did not reach the peer.
```
Thanks, this is better.
Thank you, that was actually in the last paragraph of section but it would make sense to write them in the order of events; PTAL ffa2b75.
